findings.claim: The `_Err ?? errors.$ZodError` fallback is silently dropped; `failure` calls `new Err(...)` unconditionally, so a nullish `_Err` now throws `TypeError: Err is not a constructor` instead of falling back to `$ZodError`.
findings.rationale: The original code explicitly guarded against a missing constructor. `_safeParse` is exported (public-ish `_`-prefixed API) and can be invoked by adapters/tests with `undefined`. Even if the declared type is non-nullable, the defensive default existed for a reason and its removal is an unannounced behavior change — and it now fails lazily at `.error` access rather than at parse time, making it much harder to diagnose. High confidence this is an unintended regression.

findings.claim: Issue finalization is deferred, so `ctx`, `core.config()` and the raw `issues` array are now read at first `.error` access rather than at parse time, which can produce different messages/locales and retains references to the parsed input.
findings.rationale: `util.finalizeIssue(iss, ctx, core.config())` previously ran synchronously inside `safeParse`. Now it runs whenever the caller first touches `error`. If global config (locale, `customError`, `jitless`, etc.) is changed between the parse and the error read — a common pattern in tests and in apps that configure locale lazily — the error messages will differ from the pre-change behavior. Additionally the closure keeps `issues` (which typically hold `input` references) and `ctx` alive for the lifetime of the result object, so long-lived failure results now retain the parsed payload. Confident about the timing change; severity depends on how often config mutates after parse.

findings.claim: `error` changes from a plain data property to an enumerable accessor, which alters the observable shape of the result for spreads, cloning, `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `Object.freeze`, and `JSON.stringify`.
findings.rationale: Callers doing `{...result}`, `JSON.stringify(result)` or `structuredClone(result)` will now eagerly trigger the getter (defeating the optimization) and, in the case of `structuredClone`/worker postMessage, still fail. Code that inspects descriptors (e.g. deep-equality helpers, some serializers, or `Object.defineProperty` overrides) can behave differently. Also, any consumer that assigned `result.error = undefined` would now cause the getter to silently rebuild the error on next read instead of returning `undefined`. Moderately confident these are real but low-frequency impacts.

findings.claim: Errors thrown inside `finalizeIssue`/the error constructor now escape at the property-access site instead of from `safeParse`, breaking the `safeParse` contract of never throwing for validation failures.
findings.rationale: `safeParse` is documented/expected not to throw on invalid input. A custom `error` message function or a faulty `Err` subclass that throws would previously surface the exception from the `safeParse` call (where callers may have a try/catch); it now throws from an innocuous-looking `result.error` read, possibly in a different stack/tick (e.g. inside a React render or a logger). Also note the getter does not memoize failures, so a throwing finalizer re-runs on every access. Medium confidence this matters in practice.

findings.claim: Only the synchronous path is made lazy; `safeParseAsync` (and the `_safeParse`-adjacent async variant below) still finalizes eagerly, leaving sync and async results with divergent timing semantics.
findings.rationale: Anything that depends on when issues are finalized (config reads, side-effecting custom error functions, memory retention) will now behave differently between `safeParse` and `safeParseAsync`. If the laziness is intentional, the async counterpart should use the same `failure()` helper for consistency. Flagging based on the unchanged async declaration visible in the hunk; I cannot see the async implementation body, so confidence is moderate.
